segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For I made up my mind about this: that I would not come to you again in grief.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For if I grieve you, then who is there to make me glad except the one who is grieved by me?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I wrote this very thing so that when I came I would not have grief from those who ought to have made me rejoice, being confident about all of you that my joy is the joy of you all.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For out of great distress and anguish of heart I wrote to you through many tears, not so that you would be grieved, but so that you would know the love I have so abundantly for you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if anyone has caused grief, it is not me he has grieved but, to some extent—not to overstate it—all of you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: This punishment by the majority is sufficient for such a person,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that, on the contrary, you should rather forgive and comfort him, or such a person may be swallowed up by his excessive grief.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So I urge you to confirm your love for him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For this is also why I wrote: to find out how you stand the test, whether you are obedient in everything.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Anyone you forgive anything, I forgive too. For indeed what I have forgiven—if I have forgiven anything—I have forgiven for your sake in the presence of Christ,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that we are not taken advantage of by Satan; for we are not ignorant of his designs.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now when I came to Troas for the good news of Christ, and a door had been opened for me in the Lord,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I had no relief for my spirit, because I did not find my brother Titus there; instead I took leave of them and went on to Macedonia.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumphal procession in Christ and through us reveals the scent of the knowledge of him in every place.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For we are the fragrance of Christ to God among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing:

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: to the one a scent from death to death, to the other a scent from life to life. And who is sufficient for these things?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For we are not, like so many, peddling the word of God; rather, we speak out of sincerity, as from God, in the sight of God, in Christ.

notes.note: Paul appears to refer to an earlier visit to Corinth that went badly, usually called the “painful visit,” made between 1 Corinthians and this letter; Acts does not record it. The Greek noun and its verb occur eight times in verses 1–7 and are rendered “grief” and “grieve” throughout so that the repetition can be heard. Other translations use “pain” or “sorrow.”

Paul refers to an earlier letter written in tears (verse 4; see also 7:8–12). Most scholars think it is a lost letter sent after the painful visit; older interpreters identified it with 1 Corinthians, and some propose that part of it survives in chapters 10–13. The Greek can also be read “I wrote for this very reason.”

The Greek word is usually rendered “affliction” or “tribulation” and normally refers to hardship pressing on someone from outside. Here it is paired with “anguish of heart” and describes Paul’s inner state as he wrote, so “distress” is used. Several modern translations do the same.

Paul does not name the person. Older interpreters identified him with the man living with his father’s wife in 1 Corinthians 5; most scholars now think he was someone who openly opposed or insulted Paul during the painful visit. Neither identification can be proved.

The verb means “to weigh down” or “to burden,” and the sentence is compressed. Most interpreters take it as a parenthesis in which Paul avoids pressing the charge too heavily: the offender has grieved the whole congregation, at least to some degree. An older reading punctuates differently: “he has grieved me only in part—so that I do not burden you all.”

The verb was used for formally ratifying a decision, a will or an agreement (compare Galatians 3:15). Paul may be asking for a public act by the congregation that reverses the punishment, not only a change of feeling. Many translations have “reaffirm.”

Literally “in the face of Christ.” Most interpreters take this to mean that Paul forgives with Christ looking on, as his witness. The King James Version’s “in the person of Christ” understands it as acting as Christ’s representative, which is possible but less likely for this idiom.

“Gospel” is now a religious term or the name of a book. The Greek was an ordinary word for an announcement of good news, used also of public and imperial proclamations. Many modern translations alternate between “good news” and “gospel.”

A Roman triumph was the parade of a victorious general through the city, with captives displayed before the crowds. In usage of the period this verb with a personal object normally means to lead someone as a conquered captive in such a parade, which would make Paul God’s prisoner on display. Whether Paul intends that sense or pictures himself as sharing in the victory is debated. The older rendering “causes us to triumph” has little support in Greek usage.

In the Septuagint the word rendered “fragrance” regularly describes the pleasing smell of a sacrifice rising to God, often paired with the word rendered “scent” in verses 14 and 16. Many interpreters also think of the incense burned along the route of a triumphal procession, continuing the image of verse 14. Both associations may be in play.

The earliest manuscripts read “from death to death” and “from life to life.” Many later manuscripts lack the word “from,” giving “a scent of death to death” and “of life to life,” which is the reading behind the King James Version.

The verb comes from the world of the petty retailer or tavern keeper, a trade with a reputation for cheating, especially by watering down wine. It suggests both selling for profit and tampering with the goods, which is why older versions have “corrupt.” The same image was used in Greek writers against teachers who sold their wisdom.

candidates.reason: The verb and its noun λύπη recur across the Gospels and Paul, and translators vary among grief, pain, sorrow and sadness, which hides deliberate repetition such as that in 2 Corinthians 2 and 7.
The word covers comfort, encourage, urge and appeal, and it is thematic in 2 Corinthians 1–7, so the split between senses needs one rule for the whole New Testament.
It overlaps with ἀφίημι as “forgive” but also means “give freely” or “grant”; readers should be able to tell which forgiveness verb stands behind the English.

The word recurs in Paul (Romans 5:4; 2 Corinthians 8:2; 9:13; 13:3; Philippians 2:22) and is rendered variously as proof, character, tested worth or test, obscuring the link with δοκιμάζω and δόκιμος.
It is frequent in John and Paul and needs to be distinguished consistently from ἀποκαλύπτω, with translators divided among reveal, make known, manifest and disclose.
